title: Hot-path throttle and fallback playbook kickoff
summary: Follow-up on Friday night latency spike affecting checkout recommendation service. Reviewed hot-path throttling, fallback routing to smaller model, cache warm strategies, and audit requirements. Agreed on immediate mitigations (throttle config + temporary model routing), diagnostics to run (trace + flame graphs), and a scheduled canary run next week. Action owners assigned for config changes, security review, and benchmark run.

Crestline SRE to run distributed traces and upload flame graphs by 2026-04-01

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Jonah (CSM), Maya (Crestline VP Infra), Devon (SRE Lead), Aisha (Security), Carlos (Product)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. We wanted to walk through last Friday night's latency spike, make sure we've got a pragmatic mitigation and a repeatable playbook for the hot path. I know this hit checkout recommender, so high business impact.
[00:18] Maya: Yeah thanks. It was ugly — a cascade at about 22:14 UTC, peaked for roughly 18 minutes. Payment flow slowed, some retries, carts abandoned. Our teams triaged but wanted Redwood's help with immediate rollback-free mitigations while we investigate root cause.
[00:35] Devon: Quick context: we run Redwood hosted endpoints for recommendation model r-3-512, Q4 quant, with prefix KV caching turned on. On Friday we saw a large influx of longer sessions from a marketing campaign, sequence length much higher than normal which seemed to cause KV cache thrash and memory pressure.
[01:02] Lena: Right — from the logs we pulled, eviction rate spiked and we saw elevated tail latencies in backend token generation. There were also a few 5xx error bursts consistent with OOM on the inference workers.
[01:22] Carlos: From product side, we want minimal user-visible changes. Any fallback must preserve recommendation quality enough to not tank conversion.
[01:33] Samir: Understood. We'll try to balance a temporary quality dip against latency SLOs. Our proposal: a two-step hot-path playbook. First, immediate soft throttling of long sessions and heavy top-k/rerank calls. Second, route a fraction of traffic on the checkout path to a smaller, faster model variant while we stabilize.
[02:05] Devon: Can you be specific on the throttle? We don't want to blindly block users.
[02:12] Lena: Sure. Emergency throttle config we suggest: rate-limit per-session tokens > 512 to 40 tokens/sec and apply a short leaky-bucket for top-k calls, plus an automated warm-up that pins prefix cache for sessions above a threshold. The throttle is applied only to the /v1/recommend endpoint and marked as emergency flag so we can roll back in 1 minute.
[02:45] Maya: That sounds promising. What's the expected latency improvement?
[02:49] Lena: Based on synthetic load and the trace samples you gave, we expect p99 to drop from ~1.8s to under 700ms on the hot path for affected requests. There'll be a small decline in relevance for routed requests — maybe 5-10% quality loss on our offline metric — but conversion loss is typically smaller.
[03:15] Devon: We also need to ensure the fallback model doesn't have data residency or KMS implications. Our security team is strict about any model that touches PII.
[03:26] Aisha: Exactly. If we route to a different model or change KMS keys for caching layers we need a short security review and to ensure audit logs capture the routing decision for compliance. We can't just flip to a model that's not on our allowed list.
[03:45] Samir: Of course — we'll only propose models that are already cleared in your model catalog. We'll also add routing metadata to logs (route_variant=fallback-hotpath) and persist that to your audit log stream. We'll share the exact fields we plan to add.
[04:01] Carlos: Any quick wins besides throttling and fallback routing?
[04:06] Lena: Two quick wins: (1) aggressively increase prefix cache TTL for checkout sessions for the next four hours (pins entries and reduces eviction churn), and (2) reduce model re-ranking beam width on high-latency requests. Both are config flips that can be toggled without redeploy.
[04:26] Devon: TTL pinning is fine, though we worry about stale cache behavior. How do we avoid correctness issues?
[04:31] Lena: Good point — pinning applies only to session IDs where inferred intent indicates checkout flow and we set a short pin window (10 minutes) plus a small validation check: if input signature changes we invalidate. That reduces stale risk.
[04:49] Maya: Okay. What's the rollback path if throttles cause unexpected regressions?
[04:54] Samir: Rollback is immediate via the emergency flag; toggling it off removes the throttle in ~60s. We'll provide a one-click toggle in the Console and also a curl snippet for you to run from your deployment.
[05:08] Jonah: I'll handle comms and a status page blurb if you want.
[05:13] Maya: Yes please.

[05:30] --- Diagnostics deep dive ---
[05:34] Devon: We uploaded two trace bundles and a sampling of logs (links in chat). The traces show a sharp increase in KV cache misses and a corresponding spike in token generation CPU on workers. We also saw some worker restarts during the high tail phase.
[06:02] Lena: Worker restarts are consistent with OOMs from an unexpected working set. Do you typically run multi-tenant workloads on the same dedicated pool?
[06:11] Devon: For that pool it's multi-tenant across some lower-priority batch jobs. The checkout fleet is supposed to be isolated but under burst we bleed into neighbors.
[06:22] Samir: That suggests two longer-term mitigations: stronger isolation (dedicated capacity or capacity guards) and smarter routing to avoid the cold start penalty during bursts. For immediate response we avoid rebalancing; instead we throttle heavy sessions and route a fraction to a lighter model that fits the smaller worker footprint.
[06:42] Carlos: What's the expected cost impact if we route 20% of checkout traffic to the smaller model?
[06:47] Lena: Rough estimate: 20% routing to m-small reduces token cost by ~30% for those requests but adds a small extra egress for routing metadata. Net monthly cost delta is minor for short windows; we'll give a precise number in the follow-up.

[07:05] --- Security and Audit Requirements ---
[07:08] Aisha: We need auditability. If Redwood is going to toggle throttles or route traffic, every change must be logged with who initiated it and the exact config diff. Also we require a signed policy that outlines fallback criteria and retention period for the logs (90 days standard).
[07:28] Samir: We can map to your audit streams: we will emit an 'emergency_action' event with signer identity and a config-diff blob (sha256). The Console will keep an audit entry and we can forward a copy to your SIEM via webhook or S3.
[07:44] Aisha: And KMS — any caching encryption keys used for pinned prefix cache must use your KMS key (you manage the key). We cannot allow Redwood-managed keys for PII caches.
[07:56] Samir: Noted. For pinned prefix cache we'll respect your KMS key and we won't write any PII to cache entries. We'll document exactly what we cache and the encryption envelope.

[08:15] --- Playbook and Canary Plan ---
[08:18] Lena: Here's a concise playbook we recommend for the hot path:
1) Apply emergency throttle (soft limits) on /v1/recommend for sessions >512 tokens
2) Pin prefix cache for checkout sessions for 10m with KMS key reference
3) Route 10-20% of checkout traffic to fallback model r-3-small with observability tags
4) Monitor p50/p95/p99, error rate, and conversion metric in a pre-defined dashboard
5) If metric delta acceptable after 30 minutes, increase fallback to 30% and keep throttles until origin pool stabilized
6) Rollback by toggling emergency flag off or reverting route keys

[09:12] Devon: How do we validate quality delta? We need an autop-run evaluation on a small holdout set and a live metric.
[09:20] Lena: We'll provide an evaluation harness to run against your latest holdout set — it will compute the offline metric and an A/B live check for click-through and conversion over the canary window.
[09:31] Carlos: Ok. Also want to make sure we have end-to-end dashboards that show origin latency, cache hit rate, and evictions so we can correlate.
[09:39] Lena: We'll share a pre-built dashboard in the Console with those exact panels.

[09:55] --- Concerns and tradeoffs ---
[09:59] Maya: Two concerns — user experience hit during canary and potential hit on long tail sessions if we throttle too aggressively.
[10:06] Samir: We'll pick conservative throttle numbers and short windows. The first canary will be off-peak and we'll measure both offline quality and live conversion.
[10:14] Devon: We also flagged capacity isolation: if we can't guarantee isolation in that pool, we should consider moving checkout to dedicated capacity in the medium term.
[10:23] Samir: That's an option — we can prepare a cost/benefit runway for dedicated capacity if you want. It does require a commit but gives predictable throughput and no noisy neighbor risk.

[10:36] --- Tactical decisions ---
[10:40] Maya: Let's do the emergency throttles + TTL pinning immediately. We'll accept a small quality delta for five hours while we run the canary. Schedule the canary for 2026-04-02 02:00-04:00 UTC as you suggested.
[10:57] Devon: I'll run the distributed traces and upload them before your config changes.
[11:03] Samir: We'll push the curl snippet and a one-click toggle to your Console folder and post the emergency playbook doc. Also we'll include the route metadata fields and audit event format.

[11:18] --- Procedural notes ---
[11:22] Jonah: I'll open a postmortem ticket template and link to the artifacts. We'll want to capture timeline, impact, contributing factors, and action items. Do you want Redwood to draft the initial postmortem?
[11:32] Maya: Yes please, draft it. We'll iterate.

[11:40] Aisha: For the compliance side, we'll need the signed fallback policy and the audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Also need to confirm the retention window and log format.
[11:51] Samir: We'll prepare a signed fallback policy PDF and an audit-forwarding configuration.

[12:00] --- Close & recap ---
[12:03] Samir: Recap: Redwood sends emergency throttle config + curl toggle and the canary playbook by tomorrow. Crestline SRE runs traces and uploads artifacts. We'll schedule the canary for 2026-04-02 02:00-04:00 UTC and Redwood will provide dashboards and evaluation harness. Security will get KMS and audit log details. Postmortem draft by Redwood too.
[12:29] Maya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:33] Devon: Thanks.
[12:35] Aisha: Thanks all.
[12:38] Samir: We'll follow up in the shared doc and confirm action item owners.
[12:44] --- meeting ends ---
notes: This call focused on stabilization steps for a high-impact latency spike. Traces indicate KV cache eviction and worker memory pressure. Short-term mitigations agreed: emergency throttles, TTL pinning, route fraction to a smaller model; longer-term: isolation or Dedicated capacity. Security requires audit logs and KMS custody for any cached artifacts.
